title: Quasi-finite kernel quotient factor and local-to-global dimension comparison
statement:
Let $A,T$ be commutative rings and let $\varphi:A\to T$ be a finite type ring homomorphism [def-weil-pbc-finite-type-algebra] which is quasi-finite at every prime of $T$ [def-weil-pbc-ring-map-quasi-finite-at-prime]. Put $I=\ker\varphi$, $R=A/I$, and let $\pi:A\to R$ be the quotient map [def-weil-pbc-algebra-hom-quotient]. The formula $\psi(a+I)=\varphi(a)$ defines a ring homomorphism $\psi:R\to T$ satisfying $\psi\pi=\varphi$; this map is finite type and quasi-finite at every prime of $T$. For every prime $\mathfrak q$ of $T$, put $\mathfrak r=\psi^{-1}(\mathfrak q)$. Then
$$\dim T_{\mathfrak q}\le\dim R_{\mathfrak r}\le\dim R,\qquad \dim T\le\dim R,$$
where the localizations are those of [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime] and dimensions are ring Krull dimensions [def-weil-pbc-krull-dimension-ring]. Zero rings are permitted, with dimension $-\infty$; infinite dimensions are permitted. No Noetherian, domain, or injectivity hypothesis on $A\to T$ is imposed.

source.place: Tag 00PN (lemma-four-rings), kernel-quotient square with identity on the target; Tag 00QF (lemma-dimension-inequality-quasi-finite), local inequality for that quotient factor; Tag 00QG (lemma-dimension-quasi-finite-over-polynomial-algebra), proof, local-to-global comparison pattern. These supply old item steps 3, 5 and the ring-dimension part of 6.

proof.text: If $a+I=b+I$, then $a-b\in I=\ker\varphi$, hence $\varphi(a)=\varphi(b)$. Thus $\psi(a+I)=\varphi(a)$ is well defined. The quotient operations give $\psi((a+I)+(b+I))=\varphi(a)+\varphi(b)$, $\psi((a+I)(b+I))=\varphi(a)\varphi(b)$ and $\psi(1+I)=1$. This is a ring homomorphism and $\psi\pi=\varphi$ on each $a\in A$.

source.place: Tag 00PN (lemma-four-rings), specialization to the kernel-quotient square; elementary quotient construction

proof.text: Apply the four-rings lemma to the commutative square $A\to T$, $A\xrightarrow{\pi}R$, $R\xrightarrow{\psi}T$, $T\xrightarrow{1_T}T$. Its finite-type hypothesis is the given one for $\varphi$. Its generation hypothesis holds since every $t\in T$ is the one-term product $1_T(t)\psi(1_R)=t$. The lemma gives finite type of $\psi$. For any prime $\mathfrak q$ of the lower-right $T$, contraction along $1_T$ is $\mathfrak q$, where $\varphi$ is quasi-finite by hypothesis. The same lemma gives quasi-finiteness of $\psi$ at $\mathfrak q$.

source.place: Tag 00PN (lemma-four-rings), with source base A, new base R=A/I, both targets T and target map identity

proof.text: Fix a prime $\mathfrak q\subset T$ and set $\mathfrak r=\psi^{-1}(\mathfrak q)$. The finite type and quasi-finiteness proved in step 2 meet the hypotheses of the local dimension inequality, so $\dim T_{\mathfrak q}\le\dim R_{\mathfrak r}$. By the localization chain formula, $\dim R_{\mathfrak r}$ is the supremum of lengths of chains in $R$ ending below $\mathfrak r$. Each is a chain in $R$, so the definition of $\dim R$ bounds every such length and gives $\dim R_{\mathfrak r}\le\dim R$.

source.place: Tag 00QF (lemma-dimension-inequality-quasi-finite); Tag 00QG (lemma-dimension-quasi-finite-over-polynomial-algebra), proof, local-to-global pattern; definition-Krull and lemma-spec-localization

proof.text: For any prime chain $\mathfrak q_0\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq\mathfrak q_n$ in $T$, the localization chain formula at $\mathfrak q_n$ gives $n\le\dim T_{\mathfrak q_n}\le\dim R$ by step 3. Taking the supremum over all chain lengths gives $\dim T\le\dim R$. If there are no prime chains the supremum is $-\infty$, so this also proves the zero-ring case. The supremum argument allows unbounded chain lengths and uses no finiteness of either dimension.
